featured_reviews.review_text:
The doctor was professional, polite, and explained the hair-loss issue clearly. However, I strongly advise patients not to purchase the nutraceutical packs sold at the clinic. I paid ₹1400 for a set of supplements that I later discovered were mostly unnecessary.

The strips contained basic ingredients like amino acids, multivitamins, spirulina, pumpkin seed oil, and herbal extracts — all of which are inexpensive and easily available at any pharmacy or online. Many were labeled ‘NOT FOR MEDICINAL USE,’ which means they are not proven hair-loss treatments and are essentially generic supplements repackaged under a brand name.

These products were presented in a way that plays on a patient’s fear of hair loss, but they do not provide results unless you have a specific deficiency. Instead of buying expensive clinic-branded packs, ask the doctor for the names of the individual supplements (e.g., biotin, zinc, vitamin D, iron if deficient) and purchase them on your own at normal prices.

The consultation was good — but the nutraceutical sales felt like a marketing gimmick. Please be aware before you spend money on these.

UPDATE:
Just to add to the (triggered) response of the doctor to my initial review:

I completely respect your qualifications and I am not questioning your medical degree — my review is about transparency, not your education.

However, I would like to clarify a few points because my experience as a patient is equally valid:

Nutritional deficiency is indeed a cause of hair loss — but supplements should be tailored, not sold as pre-packed kits. Many patients, including me, were not asked to do blood tests before being given multivitamin/amino acid combinations. Without confirming deficiency, these become generalized products rather than personalised treatment.

Most items in the kit are basic vitamins, minerals, amino acids, and herbal blends available at a fraction of the cost outside. They are labelled “Not for medicinal use,” which means they are not proven hair-loss treatments under drug regulations.

Calling them nutraceuticals does not automatically validate their necessity. Evidence for many of these ingredients remains limited, and numerous dermatologists prescribe only after confirming deficiency — not in bundled kits.

My intention was not to insult your ethics but to highlight that patients should be informed:
– what is essential,
– what is optional, and
– where cost-effective alternatives exist.

This is about patient awareness, not questioning your oath.

I appreciate your years of practice, but as a consumer, I also have the right to share my experience — respectfully and factually — so others can make informed decisions. Thank you to you for engaging.

Hives, also known as urticaria, are a common skin condition characterized by raised, itchy, red or skin-colored welts that can appear anywhere on the body. These welts may vary in size, appear suddenly, and often move from one area to another. Hives can last for a few hours or persist for days and, in some cases, become chronic. While hives are usually not dangerous, they can cause significant discomfort and may sometimes indicate an underlying allergic or immune-related condition.

Hives occur when the body releases histamine and other chemicals into the bloodstream, leading to swelling and itching of the skin. Common triggers include food allergies, medications, insect bites, infections, stress, heat, cold, excessive sweating, pollen, dust, and certain chemicals. In many cases, the exact cause may not be immediately identifiable. Emotional stress and lack of sleep can also worsen symptoms in some individuals.

Symptoms of hives include itchy welts, swelling, redness, burning sensation, and sometimes deeper swelling under the skin known as angioedema. Hives may appear on the face, arms, legs, back, or any part of the body. Although most cases resolve without complications, severe allergic reactions associated with breathing difficulty or swelling around the lips and throat require immediate medical attention.

Avoiding known triggers, maintaining proper hydration, reducing stress, and following medical advice can help manage hives effectively.

Carbuncles are painful skin infections that develop when a group of hair follicles become infected with bacteria, most commonly Staphylococcus aureus. They appear as swollen, red, tender lumps filled with pus are usually found on areas such as the neck, back, thighs, shoulders, or buttocks. Unlike a single boil, carbuncles involve multiple connected boils can spread deeper into the skin, causing severe discomfort and complications if left untreated.

Carbuncles often begin as small red bumps that quickly grow larger become painful. As the infection progresses, pus may collect under the skin, leading to swelling, warmth, tenderness, drainage. Some individuals may also experience fever, fatigue, swollen lymph nodes. People with diabetes, weak immunity, poor hygiene, excessive sweating, or chronic skin conditions may have a higher risk of developing recurrent carbuncles.

Poor wound care, friction from tight clothing, untreated skin infections can also contribute to bacterial spread. Attempting to squeeze or pop carbuncles at home can worsen the infection increase the risk of scarring or spreading bacteria to nearby areas. Early medical evaluation is important for proper diagnosis and treatment.

Environmental factors like humidity, pollution, seasonal changes can also trigger skin irritation in sensitive individuals.

Common symptoms associated with rashes include itching, burning sensation, flaky skin, redness, blisters, swelling, or pain. Although it is not contagious or dangerous, seborrheic dermatitis can become uncomfortable and persistent if left untreated.

This condition usually develops in areas where oil glands are more active, including the scalp, eyebrows, sides of the nose, ears, beard area, and chest. In infants, it may appear as “cradle cap,” while adults often experience recurring dandruff and scalp irritation. The exact cause is not fully known, but several factors such as oily skin, stress, hormonal changes, weather conditions, immune system changes, sensitivity to a naturally occurring yeast on the skin may contribute to flare-ups.
